title: Given a set of distinct numbers, generate all possible permutations, meaning every possible ordering. Explain the backtracking technique that fixes one position at a time.
shortTitle: Permutations (Generate All Orderings of a Distinct Set)

s1_definition.profdef: Permutations is a Subsets-pattern problem that generates all n factorial orderings of n distinct elements. The backtracking technique builds a permutation position by position: at each position we try every element not yet used, mark it used, recurse to fill the next position, and then unmark it to try the next choice. When the current permutation reaches full length we record a copy. The work is proportional to the number of permutations times their length.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a batch of payments from Rajesh must be tried in every possible processing order to stress-test the settlement engine. We build an order one slot at a time: for the first slot we try each payment, for the next slot each remaining payment, and so on, undoing each choice to explore the next. When all slots are filled we have one complete ordering to test.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill positions one at a time, try each unused element, recurse, then undo the choice to explore the rest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Permutations is a Subsets-pattern problem that generates all n factorial orderings of n distinct elements. The backtracking technique builds a permutation position by position: at each position we try every element not yet used, mark it used, recurse to fill the next position, and then unmark it to try the next choice. When the current permutation reaches full length we record a copy. The work is proportional to the number of permutations times their length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a batch of payments from Rajesh must be tried in every possible processing order to stress-test the settlement engine. We build an order one slot at a time: for the first slot we try each payment, for the next slot each remaining payment, and so on, undoing each choice to explore the next. When all slots are filled we have one complete ordering to test.

**One line to remember:** Fill positions one at a time, try each unused element, recurse, then undo the choice to explore the rest.

sections.s2_technical:
We maintain a current partial permutation and a way to know which elements are still available. A clean approach uses a boolean `used` array parallel to the input. At each recursion level we loop over all elements and skip used ones, for example `if (used[i]) continue;`. We choose element i by adding it to the current list and setting `used[i] = true`, recurse to fill the next position, then backtrack with `used[i] = false` and remove it from the list.

When the current list size equals the input length we have a complete permutation, so we store a defensive copy, for example `result.add(new ArrayList<>(current));`. The base case and the choose-recurse-unchoose discipline are the whole algorithm.

A senior-level nuance is that the elements are distinct, so no duplicate-skipping is needed; with duplicates we would sort and skip equal siblings at the same level. Another nuance is that permutation count grows factorially, so this is only feasible for small n, and we should state that limit explicitly rather than let a caller request permutations of a large batch.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India settlement team must verify that a batch of distinct payments settles correctly regardless of processing order, so they need every possible ordering of the batch to replay through the engine. This is exactly how Permutations works: each ordering is one permutation of the batch.

Problem 2 — Enumerating orderings by hand misses cases and cannot scale even to a handful of payments. This is why we generate them with backtracking, which systematically fixes one position at a time and guarantees all orderings appear.

The code defines a `PermutationService` exposing `allOrderings(payments)` returning a list of orderings. A `Demo` runs it over three distinct payment ids and logs the six orderings.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: payments PAY1, PAY2, PAY3.

Step 1: Start with an empty ordering. For the first slot try PAY1, mark it used, and recurse to fill the second slot.

Step 2: For the second slot the available payments are PAY2 and PAY3. Try PAY2, recurse, then PAY3 is the only one left for the third slot, giving PAY1, PAY2, PAY3. Store it.

Step 3: Backtrack to the second slot and try PAY3 instead, leaving PAY2 for the third slot, giving PAY1, PAY3, PAY2. Store it.

Step 4: Backtrack to the first slot and try PAY2, then PAY3, generating the remaining four orderings similarly.

Step 5: The result holds all six orderings, which is three factorial.

```
  ═══ LLD — Permutations ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Backtracking: choose → explore → un-choose              │
  │     WHY: fix one position at a time, restore state       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ PermutationService                    │
  │ ───────────────────────────────────── │
  │ + allOrderings(payments)              │
  │     : List<List<String>>              │
  │ - backtrack(payments,used,cur,result) │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (first branch) ─────────────────────────────
  1. backtrack([]) → choose PAY1
  2.   backtrack([PAY1]) → choose PAY2
  3.     backtrack([PAY1,PAY2]) → choose PAY3 → store
  4.   un-choose back up, choose PAY3 next ...

  Contract for allOrderings(payments):
    Pre:  payments are distinct
    Post: all n! orderings, each an independent copy
    Note: factorial growth; feasible only for small batches
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Permutations generates every ordering of a set of distinct elements, and there are n factorial of them. I use backtracking that fills the permutation one position at a time. I keep a current partial ordering and a boolean used-array that marks which elements are already placed. At each level I loop over all elements, skip the used ones, and for each available element I choose it by adding it and marking it used, recurse to fill the next position, then un-choose by removing it and clearing the used flag so the next sibling choice can be explored. When the current ordering reaches full length I store a defensive copy.

The discipline I emphasise is choose, explore, un-choose, with the state restored exactly after every branch so sibling branches start clean. Because the elements are distinct, I do not need any duplicate skipping; if there were duplicates I would sort and skip equal siblings at the same level. I also state plainly that the number of permutations grows factorially, so this is only practical for small inputs, and I would guard against a caller requesting permutations of a large batch.

At the National Bank of India I used this to stress-test the settlement engine, which had to settle a batch of distinct payments correctly regardless of processing order, so we replayed every ordering of the batch through the engine. I generated the orderings with backtracking and a used-array, storing each full ordering as a fresh copy. Explaining the choose-explore-un-choose pattern and the factorial feasibility limit is what shows an interviewer that I understand backtracking as a general tool, not just this one problem.
